A.explanation: Region A is curved with increasing gradient, so velocity is increasing and the parachute is still accelerating, not at terminal velocity.

B.explanation: Region B is a straight line on the distance-time graph, so gradient and velocity are constant, which is terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Region C is the bend where the gradient decreases to zero, so the parachute is decelerating as it lands, not falling at constant velocity.

D.explanation: Region D is horizontal with zero gradient, so distance no longer increases and velocity is zero because the parachute has landed.

hints: Notice the vertical axis is distance travelled in $\text{m}$ and the horizontal axis is time in $\text{s}$, so the gradient of this graph equals velocity.
Recall terminal velocity means a constant downward velocity where acceleration is zero because weight is balanced by drag.
Look for the part of the curve with a constant steep gradient before the graph levels off at about $8.5 \text{ m}$.
walkthrough: Identify the graph: distance travelled against time, so velocity $v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$ is the gradient at any point.
State the terminal velocity condition: constant velocity means zero acceleration, which appears as a straight line of constant gradient on a distance-time graph.
Check region A near $t = 0$ to $0.5 \text{ s}$: the curve starts flat then steepens, so gradient is increasing and the parachute is accelerating from rest.

Check the middle straight section: from about $0.5 \text{ s}$ to $2.0 \text{ s}$ the distance increases uniformly from about $1 \text{ m}$ to $8 \text{ m}$, giving a constant gradient of about $4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Check the end: the curve bends over and then becomes horizontal at about $8.5 \text{ m}$, so velocity falls to zero when the parachute reaches the ground.
Therefore constant non-zero velocity occurs only in the straight-line middle section. This is option B.
